author: Bill Hare
description:
Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

Continue reading...
title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare

author: Jack Seale
description:
Danny Robins follows up his Uncanny paranormal documentary about a Welsh farm with this drama. Subtle it isn’t – it’s bedlam from the get-go and at times it’s so OTT it’s unwittingly hilarious

A lot of strange and scary stuff happened in 1989 at Heol Fanog, a lonely farmhouse at the foot of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly known as the Brecon Beacons). English artist Bill Rich and his pregnant Welsh partner, Liz, moved there with Bill’s teenage son to begin again, replacing the complexity of urban life with the still silence of the remote countryside. But their new start became a protracted nightmare when they experienced what seemed to be supernatural phenomena – and the Heol Fanog ghosts would keep appearing to the Rich family for another seven years.

The case – nicknamed the “Welsh Amityville” for its similarities to the US’s most famous instance of reported paranormal activity – has long haunted Danny Robins, presenter of the podcast and BBC Two TV series Uncanny, in wh
title: The Witch Farm review – this creepy tale is laugh-out-loud funny … without meaning to be

description:
• Price beats Gian van Veen 16-11 to secure title

  • Welshman relieved after losing ‘so many finals’

Gerwyn Price finally ended his major trophy drought by winning the Grand Slam of Darts and is delighted to silence his critics. The Welshman had not won a major televised event since 2022 and may have thought it might not happen again after losing three finals this year alone.

But with Luke Littler and Luke Humphries exiting early, Price took his chance with a brilliant 16-11 win over Gian van Veen in Wolverhampton. Price claimed Grand Slam glory for the fourth time, but this one will surely mean the most to him.

author: Jamie Jackson at Anfield
description:
Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit

Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino.

This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.

title: Pochettino’s new-manager bounce falls flat with De Ligt move a disastrous step | Jamie Jackson

author: Tumaini Carayol
description:
• Spaniard wins final 6-2, 7-6 (7) against new world No 1

  • Alcaraz the fourth to win career grand slam and ATP Finals

The titles of ATP world No 1 and the best male tennis player in the world are carried by two different names. This has always been clear throughout this messy, injury-ravaged men’s season but it was underlined in the grand finale as Carlos Alcaraz ended his campaign with a statement victory, defeating the top-ranked player, Alexander Zverev, 6-2, 7-6 (7) to win the ATP Finals for the first time.

So much of Alcaraz’s fortunes this season were defined by the wrist injury that forced him out for four and a half months during the spring and summer. No matter, he still managed to tick the two most important items off his to-do list this year.

Continue reading...
title: Alcaraz puts Zverev in shade as world’s best beats No 1 for first ATP Finals title

author: Denis Campbell and Hanad Ahmed
description:
Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally

Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.

Continue reading...
title: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts

author: Sarah Rendell at the Stoop
description:
• Harlequins 21-48 Bristol

  • Full-back marks debut with two tries against former club

As women’s rugby grows, more scrutiny will follow and Ellie Kildunne has felt that over the past few months. Her performances have been put under a microscope after being dropped to the bench in England’s final two WXV matches in October, but she silenced her critics with a stellar and trademark performance in her club debut for Bristol. The full-back did it under significant pressure, too, as she returned to the Stoop five months after her shock exit from Harlequins and helped Bristol beat her former side in their Premiership Women’s Rugby opener.

The Bristol head coach, Scott Lawson, had thrown his full backing behind Kildunne in the buildup, saying that being at the West Country club would “bring the best” out of the 27-year-old and if her de
title: Kildunne returns to haunt Harlequins as Bristol get PWR season off to a flyer

author: Andy Hunter at Anfield
description:
Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast-furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino’s debut descended into an ordeal after merely eight minutes when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else.

Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after a comfortable, utterly dominant win peppered by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai, Victor Muñoz and the two creative forces. “Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic day in the job.
title: Liverpool hand Pochettino nightmare Manchester United start after Yoro sees red

author: Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn in Antalya
description:
The summit’s failure was due to a refusal to admit you cannot confront the climate crisis without shifting to renewables

The failure of Cop31 will be measured not in inches of negotiating text, or bland promises made by ministers and officials, but in lives and livelihoods, in hopes dashed and hardship endured, community leaders from around the world have warned.

“Cop31 failed because it refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels,” said Edson Krenak, an Indigenous leader from Brazil and member of the Cultural Survival network. “This presidency chose to ignore the urgency the world is already living through, turning a blind eye to the people who have died, been displaced and suffered this year alone, because of rising temperatures.”
title: Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable

author: Charlie Moloney
description:
Laura Gallacher says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand

Laura Gallacher, Russell Brand’s wife, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.

This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.

title: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy

author: Anthony Hayward
description:
Artist and caricaturist who co-created the hugely popular ITV satire Sptting Image with Roger Law

Peter Fluck, who has died aged 85, was, with his fellow artist Roger Law, half of the Fluck & Law partnership that revived satire on TV with Spitting Image, the ITV puppet sketch show lampooning celebrities, politicians and the royal family.

Two decades after the BBC’s That Was the Week That Was spoofed the British establishment and, in particular, the last days of Harold Macmillan’s Conservative government at the time of the John Profumo affair, Spitting Image, from 1984 to 1996, mined another period of Tory rule rich in distinctive characters, exaggerating elements of their personalities.

Continue reading...
title: Peter Fluck obituary

author: Peter Walker and Patrick Butler
description:
Recommendations overseen by Stephen Timms would retain system for all ages, unlike last week’s Milburn review

A long-awaited review into the personal independence payment (Pip) system will this week recommend that it is overhauled – a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped.

The final report into Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister.

Continue reading...
title: Pip review will call for overhaul rather than scrapping benefit for under-25s

author: Editorial
description:
Brussels must find ways to show concrete support for a new government that will genuinely share the EU’s democratic values

Following the extraordinary election that swept Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government from power, Serbia’s new political era has begun. Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country.

Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun
title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s new political era: a generational opportunity must not be wasted | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to f
title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial

description:
For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not

Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t.

Continue reading...
title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to articles on relationships and the age of consent

Regarding Polly Hudson’s article (At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now, 15 November), I met and lived with a 35-year-old man when I was 17. It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference.
title: An age gap isn’t always a problem, partner abuse is | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Shirley Hart urges us to look beyond the labels of ‘asylum seeker’ and ‘refugee’ to see human beings forced to leave their homes. Plus a letter from Steve Wells

Congratulations to Zoe Williams on her excellent article (Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human?, 17 November). I am the vice-chair of a charity in Hull that helps asylum seekers and refugees, and I have to say that the “service users” of Welcome House are some of the kindest, most polite and grateful people I have met.

A young man who shared his gloves on a cold winter’s day so that he and his friend could have at least one warm hand. A young woman from Afghanistan who wants to have an education and qualify as a doctor. The group of young men who picked up 20 bags of litter to make Hull, a City o
title: Let refugees work and contribute to our society | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Clincal psychotherapist Gareth Strangemore-Jones responds to an article on persistent assumptions about masculinity

Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s research offers an important challenge to one of our most persistent assumptions about masculinity: that nurturing is somehow contrary to male nature (Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so, 17 November). As a clinical psychotherapist, I find the most compelling implication is not simply that children benefit from involved fathers, but that fathers themselves may change through the experience of caring.

We often imagine psychological development as a process in which attitudes must change before behaviour follows. Yet caregiving may work in both directions. Repeated experiences of responding to another person’s v
title: The link between nurturing and masculinity  | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Steely Dan | Hot toddy | Dental advice | Christmas gifts | Black Friday

I read with interest how Adrian Chiles traces his concentration challenges back to the CD shuffle button (Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button, 18 November). The simple solution is to play Aja by Steely Dan, in its glorious 39 minutes and 54 seconds’ entirety, and I promise you there will be absolutely no skipping or shuffling of tracks.
Bren Pointer
London

• To mitigate the dental hygienist’s horror of a hot toddy (Letters, 20 November), how about having the hot water flavoure

Mail Daniel | Men’s $350m prize money boost

We’ve got Andrea Bocelli singing Ode to Joy. I can’t lie, I quite like his jacket.

So where is the game? Zverev will have to serve well, of course, and will, I imagine want to work rallies on to his backhand to finish them quickly. Alcaraz will look to end them fast as well, but he knows if they go long, he’s got more weapons. I’m sure he’ll want to bring Zverev to net and have him scurrying to the corners, because his ability to hit winners on the bike isn’t great. On the other hand, Alcaraz can nail them from anywhere.

description:
Oli McBurnie’s injury-time brace helped Hull to a dramatic victory over Brighton but the Tigers had the heroics of their goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis to thank for a result which continued their unbeaten home start since returning to the Premier League.

Fabian Hürzeler’s side were much the stronger of the teams on an afternoon they largely dominated. However, a string of chances in both halves passed them by without the goal their play deserved, thanks largely to Tzolakis, with the Greek international producing a string of sensational saves in both halves.

author: Polly Hudson
description:
What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful

I’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph.

Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)

Continue reading...
title: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson

author: Gerard Meagher
description:
The head coach said he has watched videos from Eddie Jones’ time in charge to help England begin matches strongly

Ellis Genge was so fired up by England’s powerful response to the haka on Saturday he stripped off his anthem jacket in the aftermath, completely forgetting he was not starting. Ollie Chessum told Lewis Moody, who had been invited to stand at the point of England’s V formation: “We are going long left, stay on the field and chase the kick-off.” And according to Ben Earl, who would still be out on the Twickenham turf carrying through traffic if he could, some players were so inspired by Moody’s speech the night before they could not sleep.

Against that emotional backdrop, it is small wonder England flew out of the blocks against the

author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
description:
Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama raising fears over cost to public purse

The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.

United are 19th in the Premier League and Liverpool fifth but the head coach will not accept any self-doubt. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and is keen to instil those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.

author: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem and agencies
description:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
title: Netanyahu rival condemns settler arson attacks on Palestinian villages in West Bank

author: Clive Paget
description:
Orford church, Suffolk
Performed in the venue where Noye’s Fludde premiered and based on the same text, this festive new work shines with exuberant young performers, distinctive singalongs, lustrous designs and the spirit of mucking in

When Benjamin Britten wrote Noye’s Fludde, he essentially invented community opera. Bringing professionals together with enthusiastic local amateurs, everyone mucking in to play, sing and make sets and costumes, isn’t only great fun; done right, it fosters a love of music-making that can last a lifetime. Such projects, the composer declared with his best socialist hat on, created works that were “useful to the living”.

For decades, Britten contemplated a nativity opera, which somehow never transpired. Now, Errollyn Wallen, Master of the King’s Music, has filled the gap. A Christmas Miracle,
title: Hark! Errollyn Wallen’s glittering nativity opera A Christmas Miracle is a credit to Britten’s community vision

description:
Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.

In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steered finish after the break. But Andri Gudjohnsen scored Blackburn’s first equaliser, then earned the penalty which Cantwell converted.

description:
Analysis reportedly finds striking similarities in dialogue and narrative structure between late author’s novel, Prudence, and two of her contemporaries

Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists.

The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey.

author: Guardian Staff
description:
From slow cookers and coats to dehumidifiers and lip balm, here’s everything you need to beat the big freeze for less – all recommended by the Filter UK

• The best early Black Friday deals

I love the idea of winter; every year I have idyllic visions of hunkering down under thick blankets and nursing a hot drink in front of a roaring fire. After suffering through this scorching summer, I have never been so delighted to feel a chill in the air.

Unfortunately, cold weather rarely lives up to the fairytale in my head. The reality is often thermostat battles, dry skin, chapped lips, thick practical jackets covering cool outfits, and answering the door to the postman dressed in a shamefully crusty blanket hoodie.

Continue reading...</

author: Ariana Baio
description:
Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the US in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as here

Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the country in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as North Carolina.

Democrats flipped a US Senate seat for the first time since 2008, as well as five House seats, one of which Cook Political Report had rated “solid” Republican, and four others considered “likely” Republican. Democrats also held power in the state’s first district, which Republicans had targeted in a redistricting effort.

Continue reading...
title: How did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?

author: Tiago Rogero in Belo Horizonte
description:
Once named the best player in Brazil, Gustavo Scarpa’s literature obsession has inspired thousands to become bookworms

Julián Scatolaro noticed something odd was occurring when several people came into his bookshop over the space of a few days, all asking for Leo Tolstoy’s novella The Death of Ivan Ilyich.

The 35-year-old, who owns a bookshop in the small Argentine city of Chajarí, 311 miles from Buenos Aires, said the sudden interest in a book written in 1886 was surprising enough. But this was particularly strange because when his customers ask for works by the Russian writer, they usually want War and Peace. In a video he posted about the mystery, he called it the “Tolstoy enigma”.
title: The football superstar-turned-BookTuber who made an obscure Tolstoy novella a belated bestseller

author: Tom Garry at the Joie Stadium
description:
This most unpredictable and evenly contested Women’s Super League campaign took another unexpected twist as Manchester City missed the chance to return to the top of the table as they suffered a second successive defeat, by virtue of a terrific performance from a Tottenham side who moved within three points of the European places.

The shock result came just 24 hours after City’s title rivals Chelsea had dropped points at Liverpool. It was the first time City had failed to win a home league match during Andrée Jeglertz’s 16 months in charge, let alone lose.

Continue reading...
title: Manchester City’s WSL title bid hit by Spurs after Vinberg and Naz’s late double

• Premier League updates from the 2pm GMT kick-off

Fabian Hürzeler sounded a little way of Hull in his pre-match press conference, citing the Tigers’ narrow 1-0 defeat to table-topping (and possible title rivals) Arsenal as a template for how today’s game might go.

“I think they do an impressive job,” Hürzeler said. “They had a brilliant start in the Premier League. They are very structured. Against Arsenal, I think Arsenal suffered. They [Arsenal] didn’t create a lot of big chances, and therefore we need to be patient because we also know that Hull are really good in transition.

author: Sophie Williams
description:
Utilita Arena Cardiff
Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect

Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era.

Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners.
title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe

author: Jo Dodds as told to Katie Cunningham
description:
This young man took the time to notice the middle-aged woman sitting in the dust and didn’t just walk past. He reached out

  • Read more in the kindness of strangers series

My knees aren’t in terribly good condition. I’m at that age.

A few years ago, I was at a big hippy festival out in the Australian desert near Deniliquin. There, I attended a talk and was sitting down on the ground at the rear of a large group of people listening to a speaker. When the talk finished, everybody got up to leave, streaming past me as they went.

Continue reading...
title: Kindness of strangers: I was stuck sitting in a sea of legs and feet when a beautiful young man offered me his hand

description:
The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions ponders a quirk of the UK railway system

• This week’s question: is there any way in which ‘manifesting’ can achieve the desired effect?

I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email

Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com.

When a journey is between stations that have one or more common routeing points, the permitted journey takes the route of shortest
title: Readers reply: when does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?

author: Nino Bucci Justice and courts reporter
description:
A new social media trend glorifies police and defence brutality. Many of the accounts are operated by current or former serving members

  • Warning: this article contains the name of an Indigenous Australian who has died

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The footage is grainy, taken from a mobile phone across four lanes of a Melbourne freeway, but it is clear what it shows: heavily armed police in tactical clothing forcefully arresting a group of people near a four-wheel drive.

Six teenagers and young men involved in an alleged burglary and pursuit in a stolen car were arrested during the operation in October.
title: ‘All civilians suck’: inside the disturbing world of ‘cop influencers’

author: Emma Beddington
description:
Medals, ornaments, yellow-rimmed plates – so much life packed into binbags. What unwanted trinkets am I going to pass on?

My mother-in-law recently moved from her apartment of several decades into sheltered housing and my husband and his brother were summoned to help. We arrived to find her arranging the last of 200-plus glasses on the table; the cupboards were still overflowing with oyster forks, tablecloths and, bafflingly, patchwork fabric artichokes.

It went better than this threatened: after a whirlwind long weekend, we escaped with some crockery, a photograph of my husband as a cherubic spherical tot and “Queen Alexandra’s Christmas Gift Book 1908” (sepia snaps of scowling royals holding terriers).

Continue reading...
title: Sorting through my mother-in-law’s belongings was heartbreaking. One generation’s treasure is the next’s trash | Emma Beddington

author: Harriet Gibsone
description:
The former heavyweight boxing champion on falling in love at first sight, being diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and the much-anticipated match

Born in Manchester in 1988, Tyson Fury – known as the Gypsy King – is a former unified heavyweight world champion. He turned professional in 2008 and in 2015 defeated the long-reigning champion, Wladimir Klitschko, to claim the WBA, IBF, WBO and Ring magazine heavyweight titles. He made a comeback in 2020, and his long-awaited final fight is on 11 December against Anthony Joshua. He appears with his wife, Paris, and seven children in the docuseries At Home With the Furys. A documentary charting his life, Fury, is out on Netflix on 27 November.

This was taken when I was nine, back when I was cute, shy and poorly dressed. The jumper would have been knit

author: Rachel Hall
description:
UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back

Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad.

For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler.

His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

author: Ken Ono
description:
I believe human judgment remains essential


Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?

In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.

Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice president

The training courses worth about £9,600 are being led by Ruth Turner, who was Tony Blair’s director of government relations, and Peter Hyman, who has worked for Blair, Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham’s governments.

title: Labour MPs sign up for leadership course to counter rightwing populism

author: Annalisa Barbieri
description:
You clearly love him, but do you love yourself enough to stop letting him get away with this?

I’ve got a very upsetting problem in my marriage: my husband has extremely bad breath. We have been together for 20 years and it has always been noticeable, but has got worse in recent years. Recently, he lost a tooth, which he said he knocked out, but I’m pretty certain it fell out due to gum disease.

I have spoken to him about this issue in the past, and even managed to get him to the dentist once, but he became so frightened that he ran out of the surgery. Since then, whenever I mention his breath or the dentist, he becomes very defensive.
title: My husband has such bad breath we haven’t kissed in years – but he won’t see a dentist | Ask Annalisa Barbieri

author: Philip Oltermann European culture editor
description:
Kraftwerk Berlin, part of same development as techno club Tresor, transformed into ‘war room’ for arms firm event

With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.

On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.

title: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex

title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants

author: Dan Milmo, Gaya Gupta and Aisha Down
description:
After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack

Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11.

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage. She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?

author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
description:
The effects of the continent’s coming polls will be felt far and wide – and could well turn into ‘key tests’ of the bloc’s resilience

In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.

Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.

Continue reading...
title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
Choi Kyo-jin said he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing

South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.

title: South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams

author: Polly Hudson
description:
Yes, life is simpler when you know precisely what your friends and family want to find under the tree. But bang goes any chance to surprise them – or show that you really care

If the first step is admitting there’s a problem, please consider this an intervention. Many of us need help, and what I’m suggesting is pretty much a cold turkey approach, no pun intended. The Christmas list must be abolished, once and for all.

It’s tricky to remember when it started, but, in my experience at least, this way of festive gifting has ramped up over the past few years, and is now threatening to become the norm. And it makes sense. Modern life is exhausting, and hard, so of course we leap gratefully onboard with anything that promises to make it easier. If a list is sent, or simply a direct link to one product, we can achieve with a few thumb movements from the comfort of the sofa what used to necessitate a journey, a fight through crowds, some searching, some queueing, and then a ret
title: What do I want from Santa? No more lazy, joyless Christmas lists | Polly Hudson

author: Steve Bloomfield
description:
Europe’s future will be fought over at the ballot box and on Ukraine’s frontline. The danger is that the two strongmen ultimately reap the benefits

On the facade of Stenbock House, the Estonian prime minister’s neoclassical office building on a hill in Tallinn, sits a plaque commemorating the murder of 10 heads of government. They were all killed by Soviet forces after the USSR’s invasion of Estonia in 1940.

For 51 years, Estonia was occupied by its imperial neighbour; for the past 25 years it has lived independently in its shadow. For the politicians and government officials who work at Stenbock House, the plaque is a constant reminder of the risk the small Baltic nation (population 1.4 million) faces from a neighbour 100 times its size.

Steve Bloomfield is a Guardian international affairs commentator
title: The Trump-Putin alliance threatens every European country – yet gushing populists still cheer them | Steve Bloomfield

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
Vessel erupts in flames after strike in Gulf of Finland; Nato vows to defend ‘every inch’ of Polish territory. What we know on day 1,733

A Russian cargo ship was hit by a Ukrainian drone and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, as Finland’s prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its “aggressor”. The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, suggested the incident in the Gulf of Finland had to do with Russia’s war in Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo said on X. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents. “The suspected airspace violation may be linked to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that was damaged in the Gulf of Finland,” Antti Hakkanen said on X.
title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian cargo ship hit by drone in Baltic Sea as Finland PM says conflict ‘spilling over’
